name: TGFX (Tencent Graphics)
workload: TGFX Benchmark rectangle test: number of rectangles each engine can draw while holding 60 FPS (basic Rect rendering only).
claimed_speedup: '510,308 Rectangles at 60 FPS' for TGFX versus '34,721 Rectangles at 60 FPS' for Skia; announcement text: 'renders rectangles at least 10 times faster than Skia's m136 version - reaching up to 16 times faster' and 'Basic graphics (such as Rect) rendering is 10x faster compared to version 1.2' (ratio of the two counts is about 14.7x, derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; default graphics engine of PAG (libpag) from 4.0, also used in Hippy and Tencent Docs per README
tradeoffs: GPU-only (OpenGL 3.2+/ES 3.0+, WebGL 2, Vulkan 1.1+, WebGPU; Metal in progress); no CPU/software rasterizer; much smaller feature set than Skia (README: 'a compelling alternative to the Skia graphics library while maintaining a much smaller binary size'); runs on iOS, Android, HarmonyOS, macOS, Windows, Linux and the Web.
caveats: First-party announcement (release notes of V2.1 dated 2025-04-24) with no GPU model, driver, OS, resolution or measurement method, and no Skia build configuration; the comparison is a single synthetic test (draw as many rectangles as possible at 60 FPS), which the discussion itself says covers only basic rectangle rendering; the online benchmark page tgfx.org/benchmark is blocked from this environment (EGRESS_BLOCKED) so only the numbers quoted in the discussion were seen; Skia m136 is not the current Skia and its recording and batching strategy for rectangles may differ from what real UI scenes need.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Tencent tgfx vs Skia performance benchmark frame time binary size faster' (after github.com/topics/svg?l=c++ listed Tencent/tgfx)

name: vger (Audulus)
language: C (C API over Metal; distributed as a Swift package)
workload: Rendering the Audulus immediate-mode UI on a 120Hz iPad; frame rate with vger versus with nanovg.
claimed_speedup: 'vger maintains 120fps while nanovg falls to 30fps on my 120Hz iPad because of CPU-side path tessellation, and other overhead' (4x frame rate, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Apple platforms only (iOS and macOS, Metal); limited primitive set drawn as instanced quads with analytic fragment-shader evaluation (quadratic Bezier strokes, round rectangles, circles, arcs, text, path fills); C interface usable from C, C++, Objective-C and Swift, but vgerEncode must be called from Objective-C or Swift because it takes an MTLCommandBuffer; non-Apple users are pointed to the Rust port vger-rs.
caveats: Single anecdotal first-party figure from the README 'Why?' section for one app and one iPad; no benchmark code, no nanovg version, no scene description and no frame-time numbers; baseline nanovg is not Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, and the README attributes nanovg's slowdown to CPU-side path tessellation in this app's workload; not a CPU rasterizer.
found_via: github.com/topics/vector-graphics?l=c and github.com/topics/2d-graphics?l=c (audulus/vger), README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Arduino_GFX (GFX Library for Arduino)
workload: Arduino_GFX README 'Performance' table: per-primitive drawing benchmark (screen fill, text, pixels, lines, horizontal/vertical lines, rectangles, triangles, circles, arcs, rounded rectangles; filled and outline variants) pushed to an ILI9341 over SPI, comparing Adafruit_GFX, Arduino_GFX, LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI.
claimed_speedup: README table, Arduino_GFX versus Adafruit_GFX (units not stated, lower is faster): Text 18,960 vs 97,662 (5.2x); Lines 412,026 vs 1,062,311 (2.6x); Circles 40,955 vs 118,125 (2.9x); Triangles 23,570 vs 58,843 (2.5x); Screen fill 160,094 vs 195,782 (1.2x); Rectangles-filled 332,696 vs 406,817; ratios derived from page data. Arduino_GFX is slower than TFT_eSPI and LovyanGFX on most rows (for example Lines 412,026 vs 264,950 and 269,060).
compiler_and_flags: Arduino IDE 1.8.15 with the arduino-esp32 1.0.6 default toolchain; compiler flags not stated
hardware: TTGO T8 v1.8 (ESP32) board, PSRAM disabled, ILI9341 display on SPI at 40 MHz; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6; test date 2021-06-16 (exact ESP32 CPU clock not stated)
tradeoffs: Arduino-style C++ library for ESP32, RP2040, AVR and other microcontrollers with many display controllers and data-bus classes; skips display read-back to save footprint and time; also offers arcs, which Adafruit_GFX lacks (N/A in the table); focuses on breadth of hardware support, not on matching Skia-class path rendering.
caveats: Table is published in the README of Arduino_GFX, a competing library whose own README says 'This library is not putting speed at the first priority'; units of the numbers are not stated; benchmark code is not linked from the table (the README only recommends the PDQgraphicstest example); no library versions, compiler flags or run counts; dated 2021-06-16 so current versions may differ; the test is bound by the SPI link and the display controller, so it measures driver and primitive-routine overhead on a microcontroller, not raster throughput comparable to Skia, Cairo or Blend2D; a display driver stack with primitives, not a general path rasterizer. The license.txt in the repository is the Adafruit two-clause BSD text, so BSD-2-Clause is recorded; a summary of the GitHub page labelled it MIT, which was not confirmed.
found_via: WebSearch: 'LovyanGFX OR TFT_eSPI benchmark faster than Adafruit_GFX fill rect text drawing speed comparison' (embedded GUI rasterizers); README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: LovyanGFX
baseline: Adafruit_GFX (Adafruit-GFX-Library); TFT_eSPI is roughly equal in the same table
workload: Arduino_GFX README 'Performance' table: per-primitive drawing benchmark (screen fill, text, pixels, lines, horizontal/vertical lines, rectangles, triangles, circles, arcs, rounded rectangles; filled and outline variants) pushed to an ILI9341 over SPI, comparing Adafruit_GFX, Arduino_GFX, LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI.
claimed_speedup: README table of the Arduino_GFX repository, Lovyan_GFX versus Adafruit_GFX (units not stated, lower is faster): Text 22,473 vs 97,662 (4.3x); Lines 269,060 vs 1,062,311 (3.9x); Circles 25,959 vs 118,125 (4.6x); Triangles 15,884 vs 58,843 (3.7x); Screen fill 154,341 vs 195,782 (1.3x); Rectangles-filled 320,761 vs 406,817; ratios derived from page data. LovyanGFX's own README only says it aims for 'higher functional coverage and performances' than Adafruit_GFX and TFT_eSPI, with no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Arduino IDE 1.8.15 with the arduino-esp32 1.0.6 default toolchain; compiler flags not stated
hardware: TTGO T8 v1.8 (ESP32) board, PSRAM disabled, ILI9341 display on SPI at 40 MHz; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6; test date 2021-06-16 (exact ESP32 CPU clock not stated)
tradeoffs: Mimics the Adafruit_GFX and TFT_eSPI APIs while adding DMA transfers, sprite rotation and scaling, 16 and 24-bit colour modes, and 40+ display controllers over SPI, I2C and parallel buses; ESP32, ESP8266 and SAMD51 oriented; drawing primitives only, not an SVG or path engine.
caveats: Table is published in the README of Arduino_GFX, a competing library whose own README says 'This library is not putting speed at the first priority'; units of the numbers are not stated; benchmark code is not linked from the table (the README only recommends the PDQgraphicstest example); no library versions, compiler flags or run counts; dated 2021-06-16 so current versions may differ; the test is bound by the SPI link and the display controller, so it measures driver and primitive-routine overhead on a microcontroller, not raster throughput comparable to Skia, Cairo or Blend2D; a display driver stack with primitives, not a general path rasterizer. The numbers were measured by the author of a competing library, not by the LovyanGFX project. license.txt is a collection of several permissive notices (FreeBSD two-clause for LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI parts, Adafruit BSD, MIT, and an IPA Font License component for bundled fonts); BSD-2-Clause is recorded as the main library license.

name: TFT_eSPI
workload: Arduino_GFX README 'Performance' table: per-primitive drawing benchmark (screen fill, text, pixels, lines, horizontal/vertical lines, rectangles, triangles, circles, arcs, rounded rectangles; filled and outline variants) pushed to an ILI9341 over SPI, comparing Adafruit_GFX, Arduino_GFX, LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI.
claimed_speedup: README table of the Arduino_GFX repository, TFT_eSPI versus Adafruit_GFX (units not stated, lower is faster): Text 21,752 vs 97,662 (4.5x); Lines 264,950 vs 1,062,311 (4.0x); Circles 25,269 vs 118,125 (4.7x); Triangles 16,277 vs 58,843 (3.6x); Screen fill 155,938 vs 195,782 (1.3x); Rectangles-filled 323,908 vs 406,817; ratios derived from page data. The TFT_eSPI README itself says the library is 'performance optimised' for RP2040, STM32, ESP8266 and ESP32 but gives no comparison numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Arduino IDE 1.8.15 with the arduino-esp32 1.0.6 default toolchain; compiler flags not stated
hardware: TTGO T8 v1.8 (ESP32) board, PSRAM disabled, ILI9341 display on SPI at 40 MHz; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6; test date 2021-06-16 (exact ESP32 CPU clock not stated)
stars_or_usage: 4.9k stars; widely used Arduino and PlatformIO TFT library
tradeoffs: Grew out of Adafruit_ILI9341 and Adafruit_GFX; DMA on ESP32, RP2040 and STM32, 8 and 16-bit parallel interfaces, sprites for flicker-free updates, smooth anti-aliased arcs, circles and rounded rectangles, anti-aliased TrueType via the OpenFontRender add-on; user-setup header files select the display and processor; generic processors fall back to slow Arduino SPI calls.
caveats: Table is published in the README of Arduino_GFX, a competing library whose own README says 'This library is not putting speed at the first priority'; units of the numbers are not stated; benchmark code is not linked from the table (the README only recommends the PDQgraphicstest example); no library versions, compiler flags or run counts; dated 2021-06-16 so current versions may differ; the test is bound by the SPI link and the display controller, so it measures driver and primitive-routine overhead on a microcontroller, not raster throughput comparable to Skia, Cairo or Blend2D; a display driver stack with primitives, not a general path rasterizer. The numbers were measured by the author of a competing library, not by the TFT_eSPI project. The most recent commits (2026-02 to 2026-04) are README and board-header updates, and the repository shows many open issues and pull requests. license.txt combines the FreeBSD two-clause licence for the original code with the Adafruit BSD and MIT notices of the code it started from; the bundled fonts have separate licence files.
